content:
The Lean language reference explains that Lean can automatically lift monads - that's great. At the same time, sometimes I must manually write a monad lift. As a trivial example, if I want to perform I/O in CommandElabM then I must lift manually:

import Lean
open Lean.Elab

elab "foo" : command => do
  Command.liftIO (IO.println "hi")

Broadly speaking, why is automatic monad lifting sometimes but not always possible? Is there some way to generally characterize the situations in which I will need to add an explicit lifting call?

What gives you the impression that you have to do it manually?

import Lean
open Lean.Elab

elab "foo" : command => do
  IO.println "hi"

works; specifically, it works because there is the docs#Lean.Elab.Command.instMonadLiftTIOCommandElabM instance.

Oops - you're right, the automatic lifting works just fine from IO to CommandElabM.

OK, here's an example where I really must lift manually:

import Lean
open Lean Elab

elab "foo" : command => do
  let f ← Command.liftCoreM (PrettyPrinter.ppTerm (← `(2 + 2)))
  IO.println f

If I remove the call to liftCoreM, then it won't type check:

Type mismatch
  PrettyPrinter.ppTerm __do_lift✝
has type
  CoreM Format
but is expected to have type
  Command.CommandElabM ?m.37

But I might hope that automatic lifting could work in this case, since CommandElabM extends MetaM, which extends CoreM.

So the question remains: why is automatic lifting not always possible?
In this last example, is the issue simply that nobody has bothered to add a MonadLift instance from CoreM to CommandElabM, even though it could be implemented?

Well, the problem is that docs#Lean.Elab.Command.liftCoreM is a much more complex operation than most other lifts. For example, it reset the message log such that the inner operation starts out with an empty message log. So adding an implicit lift might have unexpected side effects. On the other hand, lifting from CoreM to MetaM is completely faithful, since MetaM builds on CoreM. IO to CoreM or CommandElabM is not completely faithful but the only difference is how error message work which is fine enough.

OK, I now see that implicit lifting via MonadLift makes sense between some monads, but might not be a great idea when a lift has side effects that a programmer might need to know or care about. Great, thanks - this is the intuition I was looking for.
